missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to explain: - that a live wire may be dangerous even when a switch in the mains circuit is open
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson only states the fact and never explains it. The quotes are keyPoints[1].content "It may be dangerous even when a switch in the mains circuit is open" and writeBullets "Live wire — can be dangerous even when a switch in the mains circuit is open". It does not say that the live wire is still connected to the supply at about 230 V relative to earth, so touching it can still let current flow through you to earth. The explanation the spec asks for appears only in checkpoint 3's feedback.

above_gcse.text: A fuse is a thin wire inside a ceramic casing. It is connected in series with the live wire. When the current goes above the fuse's rated current, the wire heats up and melts.
above_gcse.why: Fuses, fuse ratings and choosing a fuse are not in spec sections 4.2.3.1 or 4.2.3.2. A whole key point and checkpoint 2 are spent on content the student will not be examined on.

above_gcse.text: A circuit breaker (MCB — miniature circuit breaker) is an electromagnetic switch in the consumer unit (fuse box).
above_gcse.why: Circuit breakers are not in the specified sections.

above_gcse.text: An RCCB (residual current circuit breaker) is even more sensitive. It detects tiny differences in current between the live and neutral wires, even just 30 mA.
above_gcse.why: RCCBs and current imbalance between live and neutral are well beyond the specified sections.

above_gcse.text: The plug also has a cable grip that clamps the outer insulation.
above_gcse.why: Plug construction and the cable grip are not in the specified sections.

above_gcse.text: Favourite exam questions: wire colours, what each wire does, and why earth + fuse work together.
above_gcse.why: This presents the earth and fuse mechanism as a core exam topic. The fuse is not in the specified sections, so the tip could mislead the student about what will be examined.

above_gcse.text: A very common exam question asks why the fuse must be in the live wire.
above_gcse.why: Fuse position is not in the specified sections, so the claim that this is a common exam question is not supported by this spec.

above_gcse.text: On an oscilloscope, DC shows as a flat horizontal line. AC shows as a sinusoidal wave
above_gcse.why: Oscilloscope traces are not mentioned in 4.2.3.1. The spec only requires the student to explain the difference between direct and alternating potential difference.

factual_errors.text: Say a fault develops and the live wire touches the metal casing. Then the casing becomes live. But the earth wire gives a low-resistance path for the current to flow safely to earth.
factual_errors.correction: The earth wire's job is to stop the appliance becoming live. When the casing is earthed it is held at, or close to, 0 V. It does not first become live and then get rescued by the earth wire.

factual_errors.text: Earth + fuse: fault → casing goes live → large current → fuse blows → circuit broken
factual_errors.correction: In an earthed appliance the earth wire stops the casing becoming live. The spec says: "The earth wire is a safety wire to stop the appliance becoming live."

factual_errors.text: Fault sequence: live touches casing → casing goes live → large current through earth wire → fuse blows → circuit broken
factual_errors.correction: With earthing, the casing is kept at earth potential (0 V) rather than going live. The earth wire stops the appliance becoming live.

factual_errors.text: Fault → casing live → large current through earth → fuse blows → circuit broken.
factual_errors.correction: The spec describes the earth wire as stopping the appliance becoming live. Telling students to write "casing live" contradicts this.

factual_errors.text: The rating is the current at which the fuse blows, not the current it allows.
factual_errors.correction: A fuse's rated current is the current it can carry continuously without blowing. It blows when the current is significantly above the rating. This note also contradicts the lesson's own keyTerms definition: "The maximum current (in amps) a fuse can carry before it melts".

wrong_terms.text: carries the 230 V AC supply voltage
What is the colour and voltage of the live wire in a UK three-pin plug?

checkpoint_mismatch.checkpoint: checkpoints.3: "A switch in a mains circuit is open. Why can touching the live wire still be dangerous?" (correct: "The live wire is still connected to the supply, so current can flow through you to earth")
checkpoint_mismatch.key_point: keyPoints[3] (Earthing): "Any connection between the live wire and earth is dangerous. Current can flow through that connection to earth. If the connection is a person, they get an electric shock."
checkpoint_mismatch.why: This checkpoint sits with the Earthing key point, which never mentions switches. The switch-open fact appears only in keyPoints[1], and only as a bare statement. No key point says the live wire stays connected to the supply when a switch is open, so the correct answer is not supported by the key point.
